front: What are papers and boards made from?
back: Wood pulp from trees, rolled into thin sheets at a papermill.
Grams per square metre — the unit used to measure paper weight (density).
The unit used to measure board thickness. 1 micron = 1/1000th of a millimetre.
As a rule of thumb, paper and card above about 200 gsm is classed as board.
A0 is the largest, halving each time down to A10 (postage stamp size). A4 and A3 are most common in schools.
40–90 gsm; translucent, smooth and non-absorbent. Used for copying sketches and overlays.
About 50 gsm; smooth, translucent and cheap. Used for designing, sketching and developing ideas.
80–140 gsm; thick, textured and creamy off-white. Used for paints, watercolours, pastels and inks.
70–100 gsm; smooth and coated so marker ink does not spread. Used for marker pen renderings.
About 3000 microns; strong, lightweight fluted layers, recyclable but not water resistant. Used for packaging. Comes as single-, double- or triple-wall, getting stronger with more layers.
About 1400 microns; rigid with a smooth black or white surface. Used for framing and architectural modelling.
300–1699 microns; stiff and scores and folds well without splitting. Used for supermarket food packaging.
About 300–1000 microns; bleached all the way through with a high-quality white surface that prints very well. Used for premium packaging such as cosmetics.
About 300–600 microns; white coated top layer with a grey, often recycled, back. Cheaper — used for cereal boxes and food packaging.
3–10 mm; a polystyrene foam core between card faces, very light and rigid. Used for architectural and display models and mounting work.
Adding a coating layer for thickness, weight and strength — e.g. drinks cartons are laminated to hold liquids hygienically.

front: Surface finishes for papers and boards
back: Varnish (gloss), edge staining, UV varnishing (high gloss) and embossing (raised patterns).
Scoring lets the card fold cleanly in the right place without cracking or tearing.
